screens.title: nodetool tpstats — Inspect Thread Pool Health
screens.narratorSegment: Thread pools are the internal work queues Cassandra uses to process reads, writes, compactions and internal tasks. The tpstats command surfaces counts such as active, pending and blocked tasks for each pool. A healthy pool has mostly active and completed tasks with few pending entries. When pending or blocked tasks climb for a critical pool like MutationStage or ReadStage, it signals the node is becoming unable to keep up with incoming requests. A concrete example: if tpstats shows MutationStage PendingTasks steadily rising during a spike of writes, that often maps to slow disk input and output or replication backpressure. If ReadStage PendingTasks is high while C P U and IO metrics are normal, look for hot partitions or very wide rows causing disproportionate work per read. A common misconception is to blame Cassandra configuration first; often the root cause is underlying infrastructure like slow disks or saturated network. Key troubleshooting steps are to correlate tpstats with disk and network metrics, check tablestats for table-level hotspots, and consider adding capacity or optimizing data model. Question to reflect on: if a pool is blocked but not pending, what JVM or GC issues might explain that behavior?

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › tpstats — Thread Pools
tpstats: thread pool snapshot
tpstats reports ActiveTasks, PendingTasks and BlockedTasks for named pools like ReadStage and MutationStage.
Why it matters
  • PendingTasks rising indicates work is queuing and latency will increase.
  • BlockedTasks often point to resource waits or thread deadlocks.
  • Compare pools to see which workload type is affected.
Example
During heavy writes tpstats shows MutationStage PendingTasks growing. Correlate with disk I/O and commit log throughput to confirm a write I/O bottleneck.
Checklist
Correlate tpstats with tablestats and netstats, check node resource metrics, and consider scaling or data-model changes if a pool is consistently saturated.
Visual: simulated tpstats output
Pool name                    Active   Pending   Completed
ReadStage                      4        12        150000
MutationStage                  2        48        420000
CompactionExecutor             1         0         9000
Interpretation: MutationStage shows high pending; investigate write path and I/O.
Common mistake
Assuming tpstats alone reveals root cause. Always correlate with metrics like disk latency and tablestats for hotspots.
Key Takeaway
Use tpstats to detect queuing; use other metrics to identify whether the queue is caused by disk, CPU, network, or data-model problems.

screens.title: nodetool tablestats vs cfstats
screens.narratorSegment: nodetool offers both tablestats and cfstats historically. In many modern Cassandra versions tablestats is the focused, per-table view providing read/write counts, latency, disk usage and SSTable counts. Think of tablestats as the targeted lens on a single table or keyspace when you suspect a data-model or table-specific performance issue. cfstats provides a broader legacy view across column families. A practical example: when a single application endpoint experiences slow reads, run tablestats for that table to see ReadLatency, LiveDiskSpaceUsed and TombstoneCount. These values clarify whether the table is large, has many tombstones, or suffers compaction churn. A common misconception is looking only at cluster-level metrics and missing table-level hot spots; tablestats prevents that by narrowing focus. When tablestats shows very high LiveDiskSpaceUsed on one node relative to others, cross-check with ring to see token ownership imbalance. Remember that tablestats plus ring together help you spot hot partitions or nodes doing disproportionate work for specific tables. nodetool tablestats vs cfstats means use tablestats to diagnose per-table latency, disk usage, and tombstone issues; combine with ring to detect ownership hot spots.. In practical terms, which table-level command to use and what each reveals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › tablestats vs cfstats
Which to use: tablestats
Prefer tablestats for focused, per-table diagnostics: read/write counts, latencies, SSTable counts, and disk bytes.
Concrete example
If an endpoint is slow, run tablestats for the affected table to check ReadLatency and TombstoneCount. High tombstones can cause slow reads and excessive compaction.
When to use ring
If tablestats shows uneven disk usage, use nodetool ring to check token ownership and detect nodes with disproportionate data responsibility.
Visual: comparison cards
tablestats
Per-table: ReadLatency, WriteLatency, LiveDiskSpaceUsed, TombstoneCount, SSTable count.
cfstats
Legacy broader CF view; useful for historical or compatibility checks but less focused than tablestats.
Key Takeaway
Use tablestats to localize table-level issues. If disk usage is skewed, pair with ring to identify ownership imbalance and hotspots.

screens.title: nodetool netstats and ring — Network and ownership checks
screens.narratorSegment: Inter-node communication is a frequent source of problems in distributed databases. nodetool netstats shows messaging between peers, including pending messages and streaming operations. Use netstats when you suspect replication backpressure or network saturation. For example, if netstats shows many pending messages to a particular peer, that peer may have an overloaded network interface, slow disk, or be experiencing GC pauses. Pair netstats with ring to inspect token ranges and ownership. ring reveals which nodes own which token ranges; an ownership imbalance can make a node responsible for more partitions and therefore more traffic. A concrete scenario: you see elevated read latency for an application shard. Netstats shows messages queued to node A and ring shows node A owns a large token range for the affected keyspace. The combined evidence points to a hot node rather than a cluster-wide issue. Common errors include focusing only on single metrics without correlating: always cross-check netstats with tpstats, tablestats, and system metrics like network interface utilization before changing topology. nodetool netstats and ring — Network and ownership checks means use netstats to detect inter-node backpressure and ring to verify token ownership imbalances that create hot nodes.. In practical terms, diagnose inter-node messaging and token ownership to find hot nodes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › netstats & ring
netstats: messages and streaming
netstats displays pending messages to peers and current streaming operations; pending messages indicate backpressure in replication or gossip.
Example
If netstats shows many pending messages to node B, check node B for network errors, GC pauses, or disk slowness that prevents it from processing messages timely.
ring: token ownership
ring shows token ranges and ownership; imbalanced ownership can concentrate reads/writes on a subset of nodes, producing hot spots.
Combine evidence
Use netstats to find communication issues and ring to see if those nodes own disproportionate token ranges for the affected data.
Key Takeaway
Network and token ownership issues often appear together; correlate netstats, ring, tpstats and tablestats before taking corrective action.

screens.title: JMX and MBeans — The observability bridge
screens.narratorSegment: JMX, Java Management Extensions, is a standard Java technology for monitoring and managing applications through MBeans, which are managed objects exposing attributes and operations. Cassandra exposes many operational metrics and controls as MBeans under domains such as org. apache. cassandra. db and org. apache. cassandra. metrics. Nodetool acts as a CLI JMX client, converting commands into JMX calls. The real power of JMX is the ability to browse the hierarchical MBean tree and read precise attributes like ReadLatency, PendingTasks, LiveDiskSpaceUsed, TombstoneCount and CompactionBytesWritten. For example, LiveDiskSpaceUsed under a table MBean tells you how much on-disk space that table consumes on the node. A common misconception is that JMX only shows high-level metrics; in fact it exposes both aggregated metrics and fine-grained internal counters that are crucial for deep diagnosis. When you inspect MBeans, know the domain names and scopes: org. apache. cassandra. metrics for aggregated client and thread-pool metrics, and org. apache. cassandra. db for keyspace and table-level attributes. This structure helps you find the right attribute quickly during an incident and confirm whether a nodetool finding maps to an MBean value.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › JMX & MBeans
What is JMX?
A Java standard for exposing runtime metrics and management operations as MBeans, organized by domain and scope.
Concrete attribute examples
  • ReadLatency — measured latency for reads.
  • PendingTasks — queued tasks for a thread pool.
  • LiveDiskSpaceUsed — on-disk bytes used by a table.
MBean domains
org.apache.cassandra.metrics
Client latencies, caches, thread pools and aggregated metrics.
org.apache.cassandra.db
Keyspace and table-level attributes like LiveDiskSpaceUsed and TombstoneCount.
Tip
Use the domain names as a quick map when you open JConsole; they guide you to aggregated vs table-specific metrics.

screens.title: Enable JMX for a lab: cassandra-env.sh and Docker setup
screens.narratorSegment: Setting up JMX safely for a lab requires editing the Cassandra JVM options in cassandra-env. sh and running a container that exposes the JMX port to your local host. For a learning environment we often disable authentication and SSL to avoid connection hurdles, but we do this only in isolated labs, never in production. You will create a small custom cassandra-env. sh that sets the com. sun. management. jmxremote. port and related properties, then mount it into a Docker container and expose port 7199. In the lab we use localhost binding so JConsole can connect. A concrete walkthrough will be shown in the content panel so you can copy the exact lines. After starting the container, use jconsole to connect to 127.0.0.1:7199. Once connected, navigate the MBean tree and confirm you can see org. apache. cassandra. metrics and org. apache. cassandra. db. A common misconception is that enabling JMX automatically opens secure access; security requires extra JVM properties, credential files and SSL keystores. After the lab, review how to re-enable authentication and SSL for production systems. Enable JMX for a lab: cassandra-env.sh and Docker setup means for labs only, expose jmx locally with disabled auth; in production enable authentication, ssl and network restrictions.. In practical terms, prepare a safe, local environment to connect jconsole or visualvm. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 5.2 › Enable JMX (lab)
Prepare cassandra-env.sh
Create a small custom cassandra-env.sh to set JMX JVM options used for the lab container.
#!/bin/bash
# Add JMX remote configuration
JVM_OPTS="$JVM_OPTS -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.port=7199"
JVM_OPTS="$JVM_OPTS -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.ssl=false"
JVM_OPTS="$JVM_OPTS -Dcom.sun.management.jmxremote.authenticate=false"
JVM_OPTS="$JVM_OPTS -Djava.rmi.server.hostname=127.0.0.1"
This example disables auth and SSL for a local lab only. Do not use in production.
Docker run command
Mount the custom file and expose the JMX port so JConsole can connect from your host.
docker run --name cassandra-jmx -p 9042:9042 -p 7199:7199 -v $(pwd)/custom-cassandra-env.sh:/etc/cassandra/cassandra-env.sh -d cassandra:latest
Lab tip
Use 127.0.0.1 binding so the JMX listener is reachable only from the host machine for the lab.

For example, if ReadLatency increases while PendingTasks on ReadStage also rises and LiveDiskSpaceUsed is stable, suspect hot partitions or inefficient reads rather than disk capacity. A useful practice is to generate controlled load from cqlsh and observe live attribute changes: run inserts and selects and watch ReadLatency and PendingTasks move. A common mistake is to overreact to a single spike; watch trends and compare before/after load. Finally, remember that JConsole exposes operations as well as attributes; avoid invoking destructive operations in a lab unless you know their effect. screens.title: Diagnosing high MutationStage PendingTasks
screens.narratorSegment: When you observe consistently high PendingTasks for MutationStage, interpret it as write requests queuing on the node. The diagnostic process begins by collecting correlated evidence: tpstats showing the pending count, tablestats for write-heavy tables, netstats for replication backpressure, and system metrics for disk input and output and C P U. Potential causes include slow disk input and output (commit log and SSTable writes), C P U saturation, network congestion preventing timely replication, or an inefficient data model producing heavy writes to the same partition. A practical troubleshooting sequence is: check disk latency and input and output queues first, then inspect C P U and GC behavior, then verify network health and replication timing with netstats, and finally review table-level metrics for hotspots. Remediation options range from improving disk performance, tuning JVM GC, adding nodes to distribute load, to redesigning hot partitions in the data model. Also consider temporary throttling of client write rates while you act. A common mistake is immediately changing Cassandra internals without evidence; use MBean attributes and system metrics to guide targeted fixes. Diagnosing high MutationStage PendingTasks means gather tpstats, tablestats, netstats and system metrics to confirm whether high mutationstage pending tasks are caused by disk, cpu, network, or data-model issues.. screens.title: JMX security: risks and hardening steps
screens.narratorSegment: Enabling JMX without authentication and SSL is a significant production risk because JMX exposes management endpoints and operational data. An attacker with access to the JMX port could view sensitive metrics, trigger resource-intense operations, or in some configurations execute administrative actions. In the lab we deliberately disabled authentication and SSL to simplify connectivity, but in any real deployment you must secure JMX. Hardening steps include setting com. sun. management. jmxremote. authenticate=true and configuring jmxremote. password and jmxremote. access files, enabling com. sun. management. jmxremote. ssl=true with proper keystores and truststores, and firewalling the JMX port so only trusted management hosts can connect. Also consider binding JMX to an internal interface rather than a public IP. A common misconception is that network segmentation alone is sufficient; while helpful, you still need authentication and encryption for defense in depth. Before enabling production JMX, test authentication and SSL in a staging environment and ensure credential files and keystores are managed securely. JMX security: risks and hardening steps means always enable authentication, ssl and network access controls for jmx in production; use disabled auth only in isolated labs.. In practical terms, why you must not expose jmx without authentication and ssl. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

JMX provides management access to the JVM and application internals; unsecured JMX can leak metrics or allow management operations.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we focus on practical observability for Cassandra. You will learn how nodetool gives quick command-line visibility into cluster state, and how JMX exposes the same operational data as MBeans that GUI clients can inspect. We’ll connect these two views: nodetool for rapid checks and JConsole or VisualVM for deep, real-time exploration. You will see concrete examples such as using tpstats to find thread-pool bottlenecks, tablestats to inspect per-table read and write behavior, and netstats to check inter-node messaging. We’ll also walk through enabling JMX for a lab environment and point out security considerations you must avoid in production. By combining command-line and GUI approaches you’ll be equipped to spot hot spots, identify overloaded thread pools, and validate whether an issue is disk, C P U, network, or data-model related. As you go through the screens, think about a recent incident you’ve seen and how these tools would help pinpoint its cause.

By the end of this chapter you will master a small set of practical monitoring skills. First, you will run advanced nodetool commands to inspect thread pools, tables, and network status so you can quickly surface obvious bottlenecks. Second, you will understand JMX as the mechanism Cassandra uses to expose MBeans and how nodetool maps to those same MBeans under the hood. Third, you will connect a JMX client such as JConsole or VisualVM to a running Cassandra node, navigate the MBean tree, and read attributes like ReadLatency, PendingTasks, and LiveDiskSpaceUsed. Finally, you will identify which MBeans and attributes matter during common incidents and know how to act on the information. Each objective includes hands-on practice or a concrete scenario so you internalize why it matters. Throughout, we emphasize safe lab setup, and we highlight security pitfalls you must avoid in production environments.

This slide expands each objective with a practical scenario and a short mnemonic to help you remember when to use each tool. For nodetool commands, practice by reproducing a high-latency read scenario and observe tpstats and tablestats. For JMX, picture a GUI session where you watch PendingTasks change while issuing writes from cqlsh. Connecting JConsole requires enabling the JVM JMX options and using a safe test environment; we’ll show a Docker-based lab for this. For identifying MBeans, use the domain names and attribute labels as a map: org. apache. cassandra. metrics for aggregated metrics and org. apache. cassandra. db for table-level attributes. Each of these skills matters because quick triage reduces mean-time-to-repair and targeted fixes avoid disruptive cluster-wide changes. In practice you will alternate between CLI checks and JMX inspection until you develop an intuition for which attribute signals disk, C P U, or network causes. Remember: always secure JMX in production and use local labs for learning.

Thread pools are the internal work queues Cassandra uses to process reads, writes, compactions and internal tasks. The tpstats command surfaces counts such as active, pending and blocked tasks for each pool. A healthy pool has mostly active and completed tasks with few pending entries. When pending or blocked tasks climb for a critical pool like MutationStage or ReadStage, it signals the node is becoming unable to keep up with incoming requests. A concrete example: if tpstats shows MutationStage PendingTasks steadily rising during a spike of writes, that often maps to slow disk input and output or replication backpressure. If ReadStage PendingTasks is high while C P U and IO metrics are normal, look for hot partitions or very wide rows causing disproportionate work per read. A common misconception is to blame Cassandra configuration first; often the root cause is underlying infrastructure like slow disks or saturated network. Key troubleshooting steps are to correlate tpstats with disk and network metrics, check tablestats for table-level hotspots, and consider adding capacity or optimizing data model. Question to reflect on: if a pool is blocked but not pending, what JVM or GC issues might explain that behavior?

nodetool offers both tablestats and cfstats historically. In many modern Cassandra versions tablestats is the focused, per-table view providing read/write counts, latency, disk usage and SSTable counts. Think of tablestats as the targeted lens on a single table or keyspace when you suspect a data-model or table-specific performance issue. cfstats provides a broader legacy view across column families. A practical example: when a single application endpoint experiences slow reads, run tablestats for that table to see ReadLatency, LiveDiskSpaceUsed and TombstoneCount. These values clarify whether the table is large, has many tombstones, or suffers compaction churn. A common misconception is looking only at cluster-level metrics and missing table-level hot spots; tablestats prevents that by narrowing focus. When tablestats shows very high LiveDiskSpaceUsed on one node relative to others, cross-check with ring to see token ownership imbalance. Remember that tablestats plus ring together help you spot hot partitions or nodes doing disproportionate work for specific tables. nodetool tablestats vs cfstats means use tablestats to diagnose per-table latency, disk usage, and tombstone issues; combine with ring to detect ownership hot spots.. In practical terms, which table-level command to use and what each reveals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Inter-node communication is a frequent source of problems in distributed databases. nodetool netstats shows messaging between peers, including pending messages and streaming operations. Use netstats when you suspect replication backpressure or network saturation. For example, if netstats shows many pending messages to a particular peer, that peer may have an overloaded network interface, slow disk, or be experiencing GC pauses. Pair netstats with ring to inspect token ranges and ownership. ring reveals which nodes own which token ranges; an ownership imbalance can make a node responsible for more partitions and therefore more traffic. A concrete scenario: you see elevated read latency for an application shard. Netstats shows messages queued to node A and ring shows node A owns a large token range for the affected keyspace. The combined evidence points to a hot node rather than a cluster-wide issue. Common errors include focusing only on single metrics without correlating: always cross-check netstats with tpstats, tablestats, and system metrics like network interface utilization before changing topology. nodetool netstats and ring — Network and ownership checks means use netstats to detect inter-node backpressure and ring to verify token ownership imbalances that create hot nodes.. In practical terms, diagnose inter-node messaging and token ownership to find hot nodes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

JMX, Java Management Extensions, is a standard Java technology for monitoring and managing applications through MBeans, which are managed objects exposing attributes and operations. Cassandra exposes many operational metrics and controls as MBeans under domains such as org. apache. cassandra. db and org. apache. cassandra. metrics. Nodetool acts as a CLI JMX client, converting commands into JMX calls. The real power of JMX is the ability to browse the hierarchical MBean tree and read precise attributes like ReadLatency, PendingTasks, LiveDiskSpaceUsed, TombstoneCount and CompactionBytesWritten. For example, LiveDiskSpaceUsed under a table MBean tells you how much on-disk space that table consumes on the node. A common misconception is that JMX only shows high-level metrics; in fact it exposes both aggregated metrics and fine-grained internal counters that are crucial for deep diagnosis. When you inspect MBeans, know the domain names and scopes: org. apache. cassandra. metrics for aggregated client and thread-pool metrics, and org. apache. cassandra. db for keyspace and table-level attributes. This structure helps you find the right attribute quickly during an incident and confirm whether a nodetool finding maps to an MBean value.

For a learning environment we often disable authentication and SSL to avoid connection hurdles, but we do this only in isolated labs, never in production. Certain MBeans and their attributes are especially useful when diagnosing Cassandra issues. Monitor ThreadPools attributes such as ActiveTasks, PendingTasks and CompletedTasks to detect queuing. Under org. apache. cassandra. metrics look for ClientRequest metrics that report read and write latencies. Under org. apache. cassandra. db find table-level attributes like LiveDiskSpaceUsed, TombstoneCount and CompactionBytesWritten that indicate disk usage and compaction activity. A practical example: if ClientRequest ReadLatency climbs and ThreadPools ReadStage PendingTasks increases while TombstoneCount for the table is high, the table likely has excessive tombstones slowing reads. Another example: high CompactionBytesWritten can indicate aggressive compaction activity that competes for input and output during heavy writes. A misconception is assuming a single attribute proves cause; instead, use multiple attributes to triangulate root cause. Always consult the MBean names and scopes to be sure you are reading the right attribute for the right table or thread pool. When you observe consistently high PendingTasks for MutationStage, interpret it as write requests queuing on the node. The diagnostic process begins by collecting correlated evidence: tpstats showing the pending count, tablestats for write-heavy tables, netstats for replication backpressure, and system metrics for disk input and output and C P U. Potential causes include slow disk input and output (commit log and SSTable writes), C P U saturation, network congestion preventing timely replication, or an inefficient data model producing heavy writes to the same partition. A practical troubleshooting sequence is: check disk latency and input and output queues first, then inspect C P U and GC behavior, then verify network health and replication timing with netstats, and finally review table-level metrics for hotspots. Remediation options range from improving disk performance, tuning JVM GC, adding nodes to distribute load, to redesigning hot partitions in the data model. Also consider temporary throttling of client write rates while you act. A common mistake is immediately changing Cassandra internals without evidence; use MBean attributes and system metrics to guide targeted fixes. Enabling JMX without authentication and SSL is a significant production risk because JMX exposes management endpoints and operational data. An attacker with access to the JMX port could view sensitive metrics, trigger resource-intense operations, or in some configurations execute administrative actions. In the lab we deliberately disabled authentication and SSL to simplify connectivity, but in any real deployment you must secure JMX. Hardening steps include setting com. sun. management. jmxremote. authenticate=true and configuring jmxremote. password and jmxremote. access files, enabling com. sun. management. jmxremote. ssl=true with proper keystores and truststores, and firewalling the JMX port so only trusted management hosts can connect. Also consider binding JMX to an internal interface rather than a public IP. A common misconception is that network segmentation alone is sufficient; while helpful, you still need authentication and encryption for defense in depth. Before enabling production JMX, test authentication and SSL in a staging environment and ensure credential files and keystores are managed securely. Keep three practical mental models from this chapter. First, nodetool gives quick operational checks: tpstats for thread pools, tablestats for table-level metrics, and netstats for network messaging. Second, JMX exposes those same metrics as MBeans; use JConsole or VisualVM to explore attributes like PendingTasks, ReadLatency and LiveDiskSpaceUsed for deeper context. Third, always correlate metrics — do not change topology or config based on a single attribute. Instead gather tpstats, tablestats, netstats and system metrics to triangulate root cause. In labs you may disable JMX authentication for convenience, but in production enable authentication, SSL and restrict network access.
